Traffic management in Cities: Skylines is pretty interesting and you can do lots of interesting stuff to immediately see improved results if you know what you're doing, and it can be pretty damn satisfying to carefully plan out a system of one-way roads, roundabouts and overpasses to bypass congested areas, but it's by no means a fully comprehensive real-life simulation.

In fact, one of the biggest problems of the traffic simulation that in turn causes massive gameplay problems because it leads to completely unreasonable congestion is how the game handles the cars' AI and pathfinding; Say you have a straight three-lane, one-way road, and you have three intersections along that road. Now presume a car wants to turn right at the third intersection. What the AI does is make the car use the right-most lane exclusively, 100% of the time the car spends on that road because it will eventually take a right turn at the very last intersection, completely independent of traffic or congestion. So even if there is massive congestion of the right-most lane at the first intersection because tons of cars take a right at the first intersection, and it would be wise to use the middle or left-most lane to bypass the congestion, then merge to the right-most lane just before you take a right turn at the last intersection, the AI in Cities: Skylines will never, ever do that because the game can't dynamically calculate and modify the pathfinding. Instead, the path between a given car's origin and its destination will be set the moment a car drives off, never to be modified on the fly, so lane changes depending on traffic / congestion just don't happen.

That said, I think Cities: Skylines is a fantastic and incredibly entertaining city builder, but that very specific traffic behavior will give you a headache at some point, especially if you're into the game for the traffic simulation first and foremost.
To be fair, traffic was also a huge issue in all Sim City games too(as it should be).

I'm always going to be a huge fan of SimCity 2000. Other entries in the series might have done different aspects better, but there was just something magical about that first sequel. Like they were finally able to make the game they originally wanted to make, and weren't making changes just to sell another iteration.

Also a huge fan of Caesar 3. But once again, it feels like an iteration before the true awesomeness that is Zeus: Master of Olympus. Both games use the much maligned walker system, where all your utilities literally just dump a guy on the street that randomly mills about. But Zeus actually let you put up road blocks to those walkers, confining them to neighborhoods and keeping them from wondering uselessly on the road out of town. Zeus also did a lot of interesting things with the campaign that I really enjoy over Caesar 3.

SimCity 4: Rush Hour or Cities: Skylines. Cities: Skylines is way too easy on the budget side of things though, but it looks nice and has a very in-depth transportation model. Stay away from later SimCity games and Cities XL at all costs.
